messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 58, Rakesh Patel had the steady, deliberate manner of a man who had spent a career handling danger by measuring every movement twice. He lived with his wife in a quiet American suburb and worked as a bomb disposal technician, a job that had long trained him to keep his face calm while his body stayed braced for the worst. The event that brought him to treatment was not at work but in a pediatric ward three years earlier, when his youngest son, then suddenly gravely ill, was rushed through a maze of monitors, drips, and procedures under the sharp smell of antiseptic. Rakesh had stood by the bed watching the child’s small arm taped down for a needle, listening to the nurses speak in urgent, clipped voices, and feeling a fear that was unlike anything he had known in his line of work because it involved not a mission or an object but his child’s life.

Since then, hospital corridors or even a faint antiseptic odor could put him on edge within seconds. The smell of bleach in a grocery aisle, the sight of IV tubing in a clinic waiting room, or children playing near him in a park could make his chest tighten and his muscles lock as if something terrible were about to happen again. He said that when he was around children now, he found himself scanning them for flushed cheeks, coughing, limping, any sign that they might suddenly deteriorate. Those triggers did more than make him uneasy: they pushed him into a state of watchfulness at night, because he would lie awake needing to stay alert, as though sleep itself might let disaster slip past him. He had come to believe that his reactions since that hospital stay meant he was weak, that someone with his training should have been able to stay composed, and that if he could not keep control then he might be going crazy. What frightened him most was the conviction that he could not stop bad things from happening to him or his family, no matter how hard he tried.

The memory of the ward could come back without warning. A child crying in the distance, the clink of a metal tray, or the smell of antiseptic on a visitor’s hands could suddenly bring him back to the night his son’s illness seemed to fill the whole room. When that happened, he did not experience it as a recollection but as something that took over his body all at once: the fluorescent lights, the cold air, the drips, the fear in the doctors’ faces all returned in full sensory detail, as vivid pictures and images that felt completely real. In those moments he would feel his heart race and his breathing shorten, and the intensity of the reliving seemed to confirm to him that the danger had never really passed. The memory’s force made him think again that he was helpless in the face of catastrophe, and that thought in turn made the hospital smell, the needles, and the presence of children feel even more dangerous than before, as if they were signs that the worst was about to repeat itself.

Over the following months, Rakesh began avoiding pediatric appointments unless absolutely necessary and would ask his wife to take over whenever a child from the family needed care. He became more tense whenever he had to pass the hospital near his home after a shift, and he noticed that the closer he got to medical equipment, the faster his mind snapped to images of his son in bed. Those reminders fed his sense of vulnerability, and the more he believed he was weak and powerless, the more sharply he monitored for anything that might remind him of the ward. The cycle tightened at work too in a quieter way: after one callout that took him past an ambulance entrance, he slept poorly for several nights, waking at minor sounds and checking the clock, convinced he needed to remain ready for danger. By the time he sought help, Rakesh was exhausted and ashamed of how often he felt frightened in ordinary settings. He came in hoping to stop feeling hijacked by the hospital memory and to believe, finally, that he could be near his family and near children without waiting for disaster to return.
